paras.text: A review of Harvey Sachs's biography of the great Italian conductor Arturo Toscanini

Ask music-lovers to name a conductor, and among the greats, they are likely to mention Arturo Toscanini. The Italian, who died in 1957, is perhaps best known for leading the National Broadcasting Company (NBC) Symphony Orchestra (from the 1930s), which had a large following in the US. Yet Toscanini was an elite musician as well as a popular one. He worked with the world's most acclaimed orchestras, as the principal conductor of La Scala in Milan, Italy, and as a conductor at the Bayreuth Festival in Germany. Harvey Sachs has written the definitive biography of this great and colorful character. Sachs had already published a biography of Toscanini in 1978, but this is not merely a new edition of an old book. In his new book, Sachs has drawn on a batch of Toscanini's letters unearthed in the 1990s, as well as the archives of many of the organizations he worked with, including La Scala. The result is an entirely new study.

Drawing on an enormous range of evidence, Sachs paints a vivid picture of the great conductor. Toscanini's first job with the baton came by accident, while he was on tour in Rio de Janeiro in 1886, after an audience refused to listen to the scheduled conductor. The 19-year-old Toscanini, engaged as a cellist, agreed to take charge only after a panicked member of the audience ran in, shouting: 'Isn't there anyone in the orchestra who can conduct Aida?' As was his way, he knew the entire work from memory.

Before long, he was leading ensembles all over the world, usually to rave reviews which he most definitely deserved. Critics praised Toscanini's interpretations for conforming closely to composers' intentions. Ermanno Wolf-Ferrari, a now almost unknown composer, once attended a Toscanini performance of one of his works and remarked, 'I come here to hear every single nuance, every bit of phrasing that I intended, expressed by this marvelous man.' The pursuit of perfection did not come without costs, however. Toscanini slept barely five hours a night and went for long stretches without seeing his children. Sadly, but characteristically of this somewhat selfish man, he did not think it was worth his time sharing his musical knowledge with them. And though Sachs debunks a long-standing myth that Toscanini once blinded a violinist in a fit of rage, tantrums were certainly common.

More than anyone else, German composer Richard Wagner (1813-1883) casts a long shadow over Toscanini's life. Toscanini incorporated many of Wagner's musical ideas, favoring near darkness in the opera house, for instance, so that the audience would focus on the music. This provoked fury among Italians who came to the opera house not just to listen to the music but to flirt and eat ice cream. Like Wagner, Toscanini also wanted the musicians to be below the singers rather than on the stage, so as not to overpower the singers -- especially important when performing the bombastic works of Verdi or Wagner. Sachs also uses Toscanini's life as a lens through which to explore broader musical and historical themes. He documents Toscanini's numerous appearances in Argentina, then one of the world's wealthiest countries, and his portrait of the music scene at the turn of the century is compelling. Musicians would compete for prestigious positions in orchestras, and fights sometimes necessitated police intervention. Audiences, meanwhile, aggressively demanded encores for performances they enjoyed (although Toscanini did not enjoy catering to such extravagant requests). Fearless in his defiance, Toscanini was bound to become entangled in politics. Tensions escalated when he refused to acknowledge accolades from the Italian government, whose policies he opposed. By 1937, he had relocated to the United States, gaining international renown as NBC broadcast his work across North America and Europe.

Some readers might wish that Sachs had included more rich historical descriptions and fewer specific details. How significant, for instance, are the names of the ships that carried Toscanini between Europe and America, or the exact mountain he climbed while on holiday? However, after perusing the wealth of newspaper and magazine reviews praising Toscanini, no one can doubt his brilliance. Sachs provides countless glowing testimonials, so many that readers might long for a change of focus. Yet, this is a minor critique. Sachs's writing is clear, engaging, and thoroughly researched. The book is easy to dip in and out of, as Sachs offers useful reminders of key figures and explains fundamental concepts with precision. As a biography of one of the greatest conductors of all time, this book sets a high standard that will not soon be surpassed.
